title: The gate that wasn’t signed
note: Fictional unit and patients. Your unit protocol, the attending nephrologist and your local disaster authorities decide every real event.
intro: You are the head nurse of a 14-station unit in Marikina, closed four days after a flood reached the water room. Four gates are signed: building, staff, supplies and cart, records. The water technician says by phone, “Readings look fine, you can start,” but the test results are not back. Twenty patients are waiting.

n1.scene: The owner asks you to open “since everything else is signed.”

choices.text: No: the water gate is not signed, and a phone opinion is not a release.
choices.feedback: One unsigned gate keeps the unit closed. The unit stays closed until the water technician and the medical head sign.

choices.text: Yes: open on the technician’s verbal OK, since the patients are overdue and the water looked clear.
choices.feedback: If the flooded water system is contaminated, every patient on the loop is exposed at once.
choices.then: The medical head arrives and stops the first connection; the unit stays closed until the results are signed.

n2.prompt: What happens for the twenty waiting patients?

choices.text: The attending reviews them by priority; the most urgent go to a receiving unit today.
choices.feedback: Keeping the unit closed does not mean leaving patients without a plan. With a handoff; the others get diet and medicine reminders and a slot once the water is released.

choices.text: Send them all home and tell them to come back tomorrow, when the water should be released.
choices.feedback: Some are overdue and may not be safe to wait.
choices.then: The nephrologist calls you and sends four to a receiving unit.

n3.scene: At 1:00 p.m. the water results pass and the release is signed. All five gates are signed.
n3.prompt: What do you do first on reopening?

choices.text: Build the reconciliation board for all 52 and flag those who missed three or more.
choices.feedback: Reconciliation shows who needs what next and measures the plan. Where each was dialyzed, sessions missed, extra session needed, laboratory tests needed; the seven flagged go to the nephrologist.

choices.text: Resume the normal schedule; patients will tell you at their next session if they missed any.
choices.feedback: Patients who missed sessions need review, extra sessions or tests; waiting for them to say so misses some.
choices.then: The nephrologist asks for the reconciliation; you build it that evening.

end.title: Reopened
end.text: The unit opened only after all five gates were signed. The reconciliation board found seven patients who needed extra sessions and laboratory tests.

debrief:
What this case teaches

  • Five signed gates; a verbal “it looks fine” is not a release.
  • A closed unit still has a plan for every waiting patient, by the nephrologist’s priority.
  • Reopening starts with reconciliation: who was dialyzed where, and who needs what next.
